issues.legal_issue: A religious endowment is public when the founder intends worship or other benefits to be available to the public or a section of the public, rather than confining them to specified individuals or a family.
material_facts: The deed established separate temples outside the settlor’s residence for a deity and the settlor’s religious preceptor.
The deed provided for worshippers to make offerings, which would become part of the trust estate.
It provided for public festivals and ceremonies, including free distribution of food and water, on a scale intended to allow many people to participate.
The temple committee was to include people outside the settlor’s family.
The deed created an independent trust to establish a hospital for Hindu females and a charitable dispensary for outpatients of any religion or creed.
issues.conclusion: The deed created a religious and charitable trust of a public nature, not a private endowment for family worship.
issues.legal_principle: Under Deoki Nandan v. Murlidhar, the central question is whether worship is intended for specified individuals or for the general public or a section of it. The terms of the deed must be considered as a whole; the location of a temple outside a residence is relevant but not decisive. The Court explained In re Charusila Dasi and distinguished Prasaddas Pal v. Jagannath Pal, where feeding the poor was incidental to family worship rather than an independent public charity.

rule.if: trust_deed_case and worship_open_to_public and independent_public_charity and public_participation_or_management

predicates.trust_deed_case: The proceeding requires the court to determine whether an endowment created by a deed is public or private.
predicates.worship_open_to_public: The deed gives the public or a section of the public a right to worship or make offerings at the religious institution.
predicates.independent_public_charity: The deed establishes a distinct charitable purpose for the benefit of members of the public beyond the founder’s family.
predicates.public_participation_or_management: The deed provides for public participation in religious events or gives people outside the founder’s family a role in managing the institution.

issues.definition: When a deed-based endowment provides public access to worship, an independent public charity, and public participation or management, the rule classifies the endowment as public.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory scheme for regulating Hindu religious trusts does not apply to private endowments.
material_facts: The respondent argued that the endowment was private and therefore outside the Act.
The Court determined that the endowment created by the deed was public, so it did not qualify for the exclusion applicable to private endowments.
issues.conclusion: The Act does not apply to private endowments; because this endowment was public, that exclusion did not prevent the proceedings against it.
issues.legal_principle: The Court followed Mahant Ram Saroop Dasji v. S. P. Sahi, which held that the Act does not apply to private endowments.

predicates.religious_trust_regulation_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the application of a regulatory scheme to a religious endowment.
predicates.private_endowment: The endowment confines its purposes and rights of worship to specified individuals or a family rather than the public or a section of the public.

issues.definition: In a proceeding concerning regulation of a religious endowment, an endowment confined to specified individuals or a family is excluded from regulation.

issues.legal_issue: The challenged statutory provisions do not take away or abridge rights guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution.
material_facts: The respondent challenged the Act on the ground that its provisions interfered with rights guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution.
The Court relied on its decision in a connected appeal addressing the constitutional validity of the Act’s provisions.
issues.conclusion: The Act’s provisions do not take away or abridge rights guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution.
issues.legal_principle: The Court followed Mahant Moti Das v. S. P. Sahi, which held that the Act’s provisions do not take away or abridge rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution.

predicates.fundamental_rights_challenge: A person challenges a regulatory scheme on the ground that it interferes with constitutionally protected rights.
predicates.religious_trust_regulatory_scheme: The challenged scheme regulates the administration of religious trusts and their property.

issues.definition: When a religious-trust regulatory scheme is challenged as interfering with protected rights, the rule is that the scheme does not abridge those rights.

issues.legal_issue: A state religious-trust law applies to a public religious or charitable institution situated in the state if any part of its property is also situated there.
material_facts: The trust’s temples were in Bihar, and the deed provided for a hospital and charitable dispensary in Bihar.
Part of the trust property was situated outside Bihar.
The Court construed the Act’s territorial provisions in light of its stated purpose of improving the administration of religious trusts in Bihar and protecting their property.
issues.conclusion: The Act applies only where the public religious or charitable institution is situated in Bihar and some part of its property is situated in Bihar; both conditions must be met.
issues.legal_principle: Reading sections 1(2) and 3 in the context of the preamble, the Court applied the presumption that a legislature does not intend to exceed its jurisdiction and interpreted the Act so that it would operate within the legislature’s competence. It relied on the interpretive approach in In re the Hindu Women’s Right to Property Act and R. M. D. Chamarbaugwalla v. Union of India.

predicates.state_trust_law_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether a state law regulating religious trusts applies to an institution.
predicates.institution_in_state: The religious or charitable institution is situated within the state whose law is being applied.
predicates.part_of_property_in_state: Some property belonging to the institution is situated within that state.

issues.definition: A state-law proceeding falls within the law’s scope when the institution and at least part of its property are situated in the state.

issues.legal_issue: A state may regulate a trust situated within its territory through control of its trustees and thereby affect property of that trust situated outside the state when the trust has a real territorial connection to the state.
material_facts: The religious institution and its temples were situated in Bihar, and the trustees administered the trust there.
Some trust property was situated outside Bihar.
The deed also provided for a hospital and charitable dispensary in Bihar for the benefit of the public there.
The Court considered the connection between the institution, its trustees, and its property to be real rather than illusory.
issues.conclusion: The Act could apply to the trust and affect its property outside Bihar through control of trustees administering a trust situated in Bihar; this did not give the Act impermissible extra-territorial operation.
issues.legal_principle: The Court reasoned that beneficiaries enforce their right to proper administration at the trust’s location or the trustees’ place of residence, and that regulation of trustees in personam may affect property belonging to the trust. It applied the territorial-connection principles in Tata Iron & Steel Co. Ltd. v. State of Bihar and State of Bombay v. R. M. D. Chamarbaugwala, under which the connection must be real, not illusory, and the liability imposed must be pertinent to it. It distinguished Sirdar Gurdyal Singh v. Rajah of Faridkote and the decisions concerning the Bengal Wakf Act and the United Provinces Encumbered Estates Act as addressing different problems.

rule.if: state_law_territoriality_case and trust_in_state and trustees_administer_in_state and associated_property_outside_state and real_territorial_connection

predicates.state_law_territoriality_case: The proceeding challenges whether a state law may regulate a trust with connections to more than one state.
predicates.trust_in_state: The religious trust or institution is situated within the regulating state.
predicates.trustees_administer_in_state: The trustees administer the trust within the regulating state.
predicates.associated_property_outside_state: Some property outside the regulating state belongs to the trust situated within it.
predicates.real_territorial_connection: The trust’s activities or beneficiaries have a substantial connection to the regulating state, and the regulation is pertinent to that connection.

issues.definition: When a trust is situated and administered in a state and has a real territorial connection there, the state may regulate the trust in a way that affects its associated property outside the state.
